Pipes split in a freeze only if they are made of plastic.
Hot water freezes faster than cold water.
Ice weighs more than the water it formed from.
check.explain: Water 'expands by about nine percent when it freezes' — the ice takes up more space. Pipe material, freezing speed and weight are never discussed; 'more space' is not 'more weight'.

check.passage: Water expands by about nine percent when it freezes. If water trapped in a closed pipe freezes, the expanding ice can exert enough pressure to split the pipe.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Water in an open container cannot freeze.
All pipes split when the temperature drops below freezing.
Draining the water from a pipe before a freeze would reduce the risk of it splitting.
Water shrinks by about nine percent when it freezes.
check.explain: The damage comes from 'water trapped in a closed pipe' freezing and expanding; with no water trapped, that pressure can't build. The passage never says open water can't freeze; it says ice 'can' split a pipe, not that all pipes split; and water EXPANDS.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: On this test, you pretend the passage is 100% true.
Then you look for the choice the passage PROVES.
'Proves' means: if the passage is true, the choice has to be true too.
A choice can be true in real life and still be wrong here — because the passage doesn't say it.
So for each choice, ask: where in the passage does it say this?
If you can point to it, keep the choice.
If you can't point to it, cross it out.
If the passage says the opposite, cross it out too.
Pretend the passage is true
Ask: where does it say this?
Can point to it = keep

example.stem: “Every aircraft on this ramp is a trainer. The red aircraft is on this ramp.” What does the passage prove about the red aircraft?
steps: Fact 1: every aircraft on the ramp is a trainer.
Fact 2: the red aircraft is on the ramp.
Put them together: the red aircraft must be a trainer.
example.answer: The red aircraft is a trainer.

reteach.hook: Pretend it's true, then point to the proof.

check.passage: The main gate is open 24 hours a day. The north gate is open from 0600 to 1800 on weekdays and is closed on weekends.
check.stem: A sailor arrives at 2000 on a Tuesday. Based only on the passage, which gate can she use?
check.explain: The main gate is 'open 24 hours a day'. The north gate closes at 1800, so at 2000 it's shut — that rules out 'only the north gate' and 'either gate'.

check.passage: The main gate is open 24 hours a day. The north gate is open from 0600 to 1800 on weekdays and is closed on weekends.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The north gate is busier than the main gate.
On a Saturday, the north gate cannot be used.
The main gate is closed on weekends.
The north gate opens at 0800 on weekdays.
check.explain: The north gate 'is closed on weekends', and Saturday is a weekend day. The passage never compares how busy the gates are, the main gate is open 24 hours, and the north gate opens at 0600.

check.passage: Every vehicle in the convoy carries a radio. The lead vehicle also carries a satellite phone.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The last vehicle in the convoy carries a radio.
Every vehicle in the convoy has a satellite phone.
The lead vehicle's radio is broken.
Satellite phones work better than radios.
check.explain: 'Every vehicle in the convoy carries a radio' — that includes the last one. Only the lead vehicle is said to have a satellite phone; nothing says any radio is broken; and the two devices are never compared.

check.passage: Every vehicle in the convoy carries a radio. The lead vehicle also carries a satellite phone.
check.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: Only one vehicle in the convoy has a satellite phone.
The convoy has exactly five vehicles.
The lead vehicle carries at least two ways to communicate.
Radios are used only in emergencies.
check.explain: The lead vehicle has a radio (every vehicle does) and 'also' a satellite phone — two ways to communicate. The passage says the lead vehicle has one, but never says NO other vehicle does, so 'only one' isn't proven; the number of vehicles and when radios are used are never stated.

units.title: Conditions, exceptions & direction words
units.objective: Read shall / may / shall not, only if / unless / except, and before / after exactly — and spot the choice that flips one of them.

steps: Regulation prose runs on a few small words. 'Shall' and 'must' = required. 'May' = permitted, not required. 'Shall not' = forbidden. 'Should' = recommended.
'Only if' and 'only when' set a must-have condition: no condition, no permission. Meeting it doesn't guarantee permission — it only makes permission possible.
'Unless' and 'except' carve out an exception. Rewrite 'X unless Y' as 'if not Y, then X'. The exception covers ONLY what it names — not the sentence before or after.
Watch the direction of every relationship: who approves whom, what happens before what, which document governs which. Reversed direction is the commonest trap on regulation passages.
Upgrades and downgrades are traps too: a choice that turns 'may' into 'shall', or 'normally' into 'always', changes the meaning even when every other word matches.

worked.passage: Commands shall provide transportation for members who are required to report for duty outside normal working hours when public transportation is not available. Members may use their own vehicles for such travel, but they shall not be required to do so.
worked.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
steps: Rule words: commands SHALL provide transport WHEN public transport is not available; members MAY drive; members SHALL NOT BE REQUIRED to drive.
'Members must use their own vehicles when public transportation is unavailable.' Turns 'may' into 'must' — and 'shall not be required' says the opposite. Out.
'Commands must provide transportation for all off-hours duty.' Drops the condition 'when public transportation is not available'. Out.
'Members who drive their own vehicles are paid mileage.' Never mentioned. Out.
'When public transportation is available, the passage places no duty on the command to provide transport.' The duty exists only under the 'when… not available' condition. Proven.
worked.answer: When public transportation is available, the passage places no duty on the command to provide transportation.

steps: Rule word: shall / may / shall not
Condition: if / only if / when
Exception: unless / except
Does the choice keep all three?

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Underline the rule word in each sentence. 'Shall' means you have to. 'May' means you're allowed. 'Shall not' means you can't.
Now circle the condition — the part starting with 'if', 'when' or 'only if'. The rule only switches on when that condition is true.
Box any exception — the part starting with 'unless' or 'except'. That's the one situation where the rule switches off.
In the example: the command SHALL provide transport — but only WHEN public transport isn't available.
So if public transport IS available, that rule is switched off. That's exactly what the right answer says.
Now check each choice: did it change the rule word, drop the condition or stretch the exception? Any change = wrong.

practice.passage: Tools shall be checked out from the tool room before use on the flight line and returned at the end of each shift. A tool may be kept past the end of the shift only if the work center supervisor approves and the tool is logged as still in use.
practice.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: A tool logged as still in use, but without the supervisor's approval, must be returned at the end of the shift.
A tool may be kept past the end of the shift whenever the job is unfinished.
The work center supervisor must approve every tool checkout.
A tool may be used on the flight line before it is checked out if it is returned the same shift.
practice.explain: A tool may be kept 'only if the work center supervisor approves AND the tool is logged' — logging without approval fails the condition. An unfinished job is not the condition; supervisors approve keeping tools late, not every checkout; and tools are checked out 'before use'.

practice.passage: Safety goggles shall be worn when operating grinding equipment. A face shield may be worn over the goggles for added protection but shall not be used in place of them.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A face shield alone gives adequate protection when grinding.
A face shield must be worn whenever goggles are worn.
Goggles are required during grinding whether or not a face shield is worn.
Goggles may be skipped if a grinding job lasts less than a minute.
practice.explain: Goggles 'shall be worn', and a face shield 'shall not be used in place of them'. A shield alone is exactly what's forbidden; the shield is optional ('may'), not required; and no time-based exception exists.

practice.passage: Space-available passengers may be carried on squadron aircraft unless the flight involves aerial refueling, low-level flight or weapons release. Passengers shall be briefed on emergency egress before every flight on which they are carried.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Passengers may be carried on a low-level flight if they have been briefed on egress.
A passenger who flew yesterday need not be briefed again today.
Space-available passengers must be carried whenever seats are open.
The passage does not bar space-available passengers from a routine flight with no refueling, low-level flight or weapons release.
practice.explain: Passengers 'may be carried… unless' one of three activities is involved; a flight with none of them hits no exception. The briefing doesn't override the low-level exception; it is required 'before every flight'; and 'may be carried' is permission, not a requirement.

practice.passage: Squadron instructions shall be consistent with wing instructions, and wing instructions shall be consistent with type commander directives. Where a squadron instruction conflicts with a type commander directive, the type commander directive governs.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Wing instructions must conform to squadron instructions.
On the point of conflict, a squadron instruction that conflicts with a type commander directive does not govern.
Type commander directives must be consistent with wing instructions.
A squadron instruction may override a wing instruction if the squadron commander approves.
practice.explain: 'Where a squadron instruction conflicts with a type commander directive, the type commander directive governs.' The chain runs squadron → wing → type commander: the first and third choices reverse it, and no override by squadron approval exists.

practice.passage: Night flight operations shall not be conducted unless a rescue helicopter is airborne or on alert to launch within five minutes. When no rescue helicopter is available, the commanding officer may authorize night operations only if a surface vessel capable of recovering aircrew is stationed in the operating area.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Night operations may never proceed without a rescue helicopter.
With a rescue helicopter on five-minute alert, the commanding officer must still authorize night operations.
If no rescue helicopter is available, a suitable surface vessel in the operating area is a requirement for night operations.
A surface vessel may replace the rescue helicopter whenever the commanding officer prefers.
practice.explain: Without a helicopter, the CO may authorize night operations 'only if a surface vessel… is stationed in the operating area' — the vessel is a must-have. The exception shows night ops CAN proceed without a helicopter; CO authorization is tied to the no-helicopter case; and the substitution applies 'when no rescue helicopter is available', not at preference.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's turn every rule into a plain 'if… then…' sentence before looking at the choices.
steps: Rewrite 'X unless Y' as: 'If NOT Y, then X.' Rewrite 'X only if Y' as: 'No Y → no X.'
Rewrite 'X may be done' as: 'X is allowed — nobody has to.' Rewrite 'X shall not' as: 'X is banned.'
Write the exception next to the rule it belongs to. It covers that rule and nothing else.
Now test each choice against your if-then sentences. Did it drop the 'if'? Flip the 'then'? Move the exception to another rule?
A choice that keeps every 'if', 'then' and 'unless' intact is the survivor.
X unless Y
= if NOT Y, then X
X only if Y
= no Y, no X

example.stem: “Hearing protection is required in the engine room unless the plant is shut down.” The plant is shut down. What does the rule say about hearing protection?
steps: Rewrite: if the plant is NOT shut down, hearing protection is required.
The plant IS shut down, so the 'if' is false — the requirement doesn't switch on.
Careful: the rule doesn't BAN protection either. It just doesn't require it.
example.answer: It is not required by this rule — though it isn't forbidden.

reteach.hook: Turn it into if-then, then check nothing got flipped.

check.passage: In this port, liberty is granted only to members who travel in pairs. Members in pay grade E-7 or above may go ashore alone.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: An E-4 may go ashore alone with a petty officer's approval.
An E-8 is not required to travel with a partner.
Members traveling in pairs must both be E-7 or above.
check.explain: 'Members in pay grade E-7 or above may go ashore alone' — an E-8 qualifies. No approval route exists for an E-4; 'may go alone' is a permission, not a requirement; and pairs can be any grade.

check.passage: In this port, liberty is granted only to members who travel in pairs. Members in pay grade E-7 or above may go ashore alone.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: E-7s are the only members granted liberty in this port.
Liberty is denied to all members in this port.
Each pair going ashore must include at least one E-7.
An E-5 going ashore alone would be breaking the rule.
check.explain: Liberty is granted 'only to members who travel in pairs', with the exception limited to E-7 and above; an E-5 alone fits neither. Liberty is granted to pairs of any grade, and nothing requires an E-7 in each pair.

check.passage: Aircraft shall be armed only in designated arming areas. Arming in any other location requires the approval of the air officer, which may be given only if the designated area is unusable.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: If the designated arming area can be used, the air officer may not properly approve arming elsewhere.
The air officer may approve arming outside the designated area whenever it is convenient.
Aircraft are normally armed outside the designated area.
The designated arming area is chosen by the air officer.
check.explain: Approval 'may be given only if the designated area is unusable' — a usable area means no approval. Convenience is not the condition; aircraft 'shall be armed only in designated arming areas' by default; and the passage never says who designates the area.

check.passage: Aircraft shall be armed only in designated arming areas. Arming in any other location requires the approval of the air officer, which may be given only if the designated area is unusable.
check.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: An unusable arming area automatically permits arming anywhere.
Any officer present may approve arming outside the designated area.
Arming outside a designated area cannot properly take place without the air officer's approval.
The air officer must approve every arming, including arming in the designated area.
check.explain: Arming elsewhere 'requires the approval of the air officer'. An unusable area only makes approval POSSIBLE — it is still needed, so 'automatically' fails; only the air officer is named; and approval is required for other locations, not the designated one.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: 'Shall' and 'must' mean you have to.
'May' means you are allowed to, but you don't have to.
'Shall not' means you are not allowed to.
'Unless' means 'except if'.
'Only if' means it can't happen without that thing.
Find these words first in every sentence.
Then check that the choice uses the SAME word.
If a choice changes 'may' to 'must', or drops an 'unless', it's wrong.
shall / must = have to
may = allowed
shall not = not allowed

example.stem: “You may leave early only if your work is finished.” Your work is not finished. May you leave early?
steps: 'Only if' means you can't leave early without finished work.
Your work is not finished.
So you may not leave early.

reteach.hook: Find the small rule words, and make sure the choice didn't change them.

check.passage: Sailors may wear civilian clothes ashore. Aboard ship, they shall wear the uniform of the day unless they are departing on or returning from liberty.
check.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Sailors must wear civilian clothes ashore.
A sailor returning from liberty may be aboard in civilian clothes.
Sailors may never wear uniforms ashore.
Uniforms are optional aboard ship at all times.
check.explain: Aboard, the uniform is required 'unless they are departing on or returning from liberty' — so a returning sailor may be in civilian clothes. 'May wear civilian clothes ashore' is allowed, not required, and doesn't forbid uniforms; and aboard ship the uniform 'shall' be worn outside the exception.

check.passage: Sailors may wear civilian clothes ashore. Aboard ship, they shall wear the uniform of the day unless they are departing on or returning from liberty.
check.stem: In the passage, the word 'may' tells you that wearing civilian clothes ashore is —
check.explain: 'May' gives permission without requiring anything. Nothing in the passage limits it to officers.

check.passage: Visitors may enter the base only if they hold a valid pass. Passes are issued at the visitor center outside the main gate.
check.stem: A visitor arrives at the base without a pass. Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: The visitor may enter if escorted by a sailor.
The visitor may enter for up to one hour.
The visitor must leave the area permanently.
The visitor may not enter the base without first getting a pass.
check.explain: Visitors may enter 'only if they hold a valid pass'. No escort or time-limited exception is given, and nothing says the visitor must leave for good — they can get a pass at the visitor center.

check.passage: Visitors may enter the base only if they hold a valid pass. Passes are issued at the visitor center outside the main gate.
check.stem: Assuming the passage is true, which statement must also be true?
options: A visitor who entered the base held a valid pass.
Holding a pass guarantees a visitor entry to the base.
Every visitor already has a pass.
The visitor center is inside the base.
check.explain: 'Only if' means entry can't happen without a pass, so anyone who entered had one. But 'only if' doesn't make a pass a guarantee; nothing says every visitor has one; and the visitor center is 'outside the main gate'.

units.title: Over-claims & scope traps
units.objective: Match the strength and the subject of every choice to the passage — no stretching 'usually' into 'always', and no swapping who, where or when.

steps: Extreme words — all, every, always, never, only, none, proves — make a choice easy to break. One counter-example in the passage kills it.
Hedged words in the passage (usually, normally, may, can, generally, most, often) must stay hedged in the answer. 'Usually' never supports 'always'; 'most' never supports 'all'.
Scope shifts swap the subject: the passage is about aircrew on OVERWATER flights; the choice talks about all aircrew, or the whole squadron. Check the who, what, where and when match.
Comparisons are scope traps too: 'the most', 'the best', 'more than', 'the leading cause'. Unless the passage compares, the choice can't.
Don't over-correct. An extreme word is fine if the passage is equally extreme: 'shall not under any circumstances' DOES support 'never'. Match strength — don't just fear big words.

worked.passage: Aircrew assigned to overwater flights shall complete water survival training every four years. Aircrew who have not completed the training within that period shall not be scheduled for overwater flights until they requalify.
worked.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
steps: Who is covered? Aircrew ASSIGNED TO OVERWATER FLIGHTS. What? Training every four years. Penalty? Not scheduled for overwater flights until requalified.
'All aircrew must complete water survival training every four years.' Scope shift — 'all aircrew' is bigger than 'aircrew assigned to overwater flights'. Out.
'Water survival training is the most important training aircrew receive.' A comparison the passage never makes. Out.
'Aircrew who are overdue are barred from all flying until they requalify.' Scope shift — the bar covers overwater flights only. Out.

'An overwater pilot whose last water survival training was five years ago must requalify before flying an overwater mission.' Five years is beyond the four-year period, and the penalty is exactly overwater scheduling. Proven.
worked.answer: An overwater pilot whose last water survival training was five years ago must requalify before flying an overwater mission.

visual.caption: A choice may not climb higher up the ladder than the passage does

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Find the 'how much' word in each choice: all, most, some, never, always, usually.
Find the matching word in the passage.
Put them side by side. If the choice says 'all' and the passage says 'most', the choice went too far. Out.
Next, find WHO or WHAT each choice is about. Here: aircrew on overwater flights.
If a choice talks about a bigger group (all aircrew) or a different thing (all flying), it changed the subject. Out.
The answer left standing has the same strength AND the same subject as the passage.

practice.passage: Members are normally required to complete a periodic health assessment each year. Members who are deployed when their assessment falls due shall complete it within 30 days of returning.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Every member completes a health assessment exactly once a year.
A deployed member's assessment can be completed after its usual due date.
Deployed members are excused from periodic health assessments.
The health assessment is the most important part of medical readiness.
practice.explain: A member deployed when it 'falls due' completes it 'within 30 days of returning' — after the due date. 'Normally' does not support 'exactly' for every member; deployed members are delayed, not excused; and nothing is ranked 'most important'.

practice.passage: Lookouts on the bridge wings report all contacts to the officer of the deck. At night, lookouts are rotated at least every hour, because the ability to detect faint lights declines with time on watch.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Lookouts report only surface contacts that are on a collision course.
A lookout's ability to detect faint lights is the same at the end of a watch as at the start.
Lookouts are rotated at least every hour by day as well as by night.
A night lookout relieved after 45 minutes would not break the rotation rule.
practice.explain: At night lookouts rotate 'at least every hour' — 45 minutes is within that. They report 'all contacts', not only some; detection 'declines with time on watch'; and the hourly rule is stated for night only — applying it to daytime is a scope shift.

practice.passage: Most of the lightning that strikes the ground carries a negative charge, but a small fraction carries a positive charge. Positive strikes typically carry more current and last longer, and they can occur many miles from the storm that produces them, sometimes under clear skies.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Every positive strike carries more current than any negative strike.
Positive lightning strikes the ground more often than negative lightning.
Being outside the area of a storm does not always mean being safe from its lightning.
All lightning that strikes the ground carries a negative charge.
practice.explain: Positive strikes 'can occur many miles from the storm… sometimes under clear skies'. 'Typically' does not support 'every'; 'a small fraction' is positive, so positive strikes are LESS common; and 'most', not all, is negative.

practice.passage: Engine compressor washes shall be performed at the intervals in the maintenance plan. For aircraft operating in a salt-laden environment, washes shall be performed more frequently, as directed by the squadron maintenance officer.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: All aircraft receive compressor washes at the same interval.
The maintenance officer may reduce wash frequency for aircraft operating in salt-laden air.
An aircraft operating in salt-laden air is washed more often than the plan's normal interval.
Salt is the leading cause of engine failure.
practice.explain: In salt-laden environments 'washes shall be performed more frequently'. That rules out 'the same interval' for all aircraft; the maintenance officer directs MORE washes, not fewer; and 'leading cause of engine failure' is a comparison never made.

practice.passage: Most of the ship's crew live in base housing or within 20 miles of the base. Members who live more than 50 miles from the base shall notify their division officer, because recall times for the ship are calculated on the assumption that the crew can report within two hours.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: All members of the crew live within 20 miles of the base.
A member living 60 miles from the base has a notification duty that a member living 15 miles away does not.
Members who live 30 miles from the base must notify their division officer.
Members who live more than 50 miles away cannot report within two hours.
practice.explain: Only members 'more than 50 miles from the base shall notify'; 60 miles qualifies and 15 does not. 'Most', not all, live within 20 miles; 30 miles is under the 50-mile trigger; and the passage says recall times ASSUME a two-hour report — it never says distant members cannot make it.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's measure every choice on a strength ladder and a subject check.
steps: Picture a ladder: none → few → some → many → most → all. Never → seldom → sometimes → often → usually → always.
Find the passage's rung. A choice may stand on the same rung or lower — never higher.
'Most sailors are trained' supports 'some sailors are trained' (lower rung), but not 'all sailors are trained' (higher rung).
Then do the subject check: same who, same where, same when? 'At night' doesn't stretch to 'day and night'; 'overwater flights' doesn't stretch to 'all flights'.
Fail either check and the choice is out.

visual.caption: Stay on the passage's rung — or below it

example.stem: “Most sailors on the ship have completed firefighting training.” Which follows: (a) all sailors are trained, or (b) some sailors are trained?
steps: The passage's rung: most.
(a) 'All' is a higher rung. Out.
(b) 'Some' is a lower rung — if most are trained, some certainly are. Keep.

reteach.hook: Same rung or lower, same subject — or it's out.

check.passage: General quarters drills are usually held twice a week while the ship is underway. In port, drills are held at the commanding officer's discretion.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: General quarters drills are always held twice a week.
Drills are never held while the ship is in port.
In port, the commanding officer decides when drills are held.
The ship spends most of the year underway.
check.explain: In port, drills are 'at the commanding officer's discretion'. 'Usually' does not support 'always'; in-port drills are at the CO's discretion, not banned; and time underway is never mentioned.

check.passage: General quarters drills are usually held twice a week while the ship is underway. In port, drills are held at the commanding officer's discretion.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Drills in port are held more often than drills underway.
Under the passage, an underway week with only one general quarters drill is possible.
Every underway week includes exactly two drills.
In-port drills are forbidden on weekends.
check.explain: Drills are 'usually' held twice a week underway — 'usually' leaves room for weeks that differ. The passage never compares in-port frequency, doesn't promise 'exactly two' every week, and says nothing about weekends.

check.passage: Many bird species migrate south in the autumn, and some travel thousands of miles. Migration is often triggered by shortening day length rather than by falling temperature.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: All bird species migrate south in the autumn.
Every migrating bird travels thousands of miles.
Falling temperature is the only trigger of migration.
A bird might begin migrating before the weather turns cold.
check.explain: Migration is 'often triggered by shortening day length rather than by falling temperature', so a bird may set off before it's cold. 'Many species' is not all; 'some travel thousands of miles' is not every bird; and temperature is not called the only trigger.

check.passage: Many bird species migrate south in the autumn, and some travel thousands of miles. Migration is often triggered by shortening day length rather than by falling temperature.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Day length plays a part in when at least some birds migrate.
Birds that do not migrate die in winter.
Most migrating birds travel thousands of miles.
Migration is always triggered by day length.
check.explain: Migration is 'often triggered by shortening day length' — 'often' supports 'at least some'. Non-migrating birds are never discussed; 'some' doesn't climb to 'most'; and 'often' doesn't climb to 'always'.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Some words tell you HOW MANY or HOW OFTEN.
'All' means every single one. 'None' means not one.
'Most' means more than half. 'Some' means at least one.
'Always' means every time. 'Never' means not once. 'Usually' means most of the time.
Find the how-many word in the passage.
Find the how-many word in the choice.
If the choice says MORE than the passage, it's wrong.
Saying 'all' when the passage says 'most' is the most common mistake.

example.stem: “Some of the jets on the ramp are F/A-18s.” Can you say that all the jets are F/A-18s? Can you say that at least one is?
steps: 'Some' means at least one.
So at least one jet is an F/A-18 — yes.
But 'some' is not 'all', so you can't say they all are.
example.answer: At least one is an F/A-18; you can't say they all are.

reteach.hook: Never let the choice say more than the passage does.

check.passage: Most members of the helicopter detachment are qualified swimmers. All rescue swimmers in the detachment have completed advanced training.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Every member of the detachment is a qualified swimmer.
No one in the detachment has completed advanced training.
Any rescue swimmer in the detachment has completed advanced training.
Most of the detachment are rescue swimmers.
check.explain: 'All rescue swimmers in the detachment have completed advanced training' — so any one of them has. 'Most' doesn't become 'every'; rescue swimmers HAVE the training; and the passage never says how many rescue swimmers there are.

check.passage: Most members of the helicopter detachment are qualified swimmers. All rescue swimmers in the detachment have completed advanced training.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Some members of the detachment may not be qualified swimmers.
All qualified swimmers in the detachment are rescue swimmers.
Advanced training is required for every member of the detachment.
Rescue swimmers make up half of the detachment.
check.explain: 'Most' members are qualified swimmers — 'most' leaves room for some who aren't. The passage says all rescue swimmers have advanced training, not that all swimmers are rescue swimmers; and no one else is said to need advanced training or to make up half.

check.passage: In this region, afternoon thunderstorms occur on most summer days. They seldom occur in winter.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Thunderstorms never occur here in winter.
Afternoon thunderstorms occur here every summer day.
On a summer afternoon here, a thunderstorm is more likely than not.
Winter is the stormiest season in this region.
check.explain: Afternoon storms occur 'on most summer days' — more than half, so more likely than not. 'Seldom' isn't 'never'; 'most' isn't 'every'; and winter storms are seldom, so winter can't be the stormiest.

check.passage: In this region, afternoon thunderstorms occur on most summer days. They seldom occur in winter.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Summer is the only season with thunderstorms here.
A winter thunderstorm here is possible but uncommon.
Morning thunderstorms are common here in summer.
The thunderstorms here are caused by the ocean.
check.explain: 'Seldom' means it happens, but not often. Winter storms exist (seldom), so summer isn't the only season; the passage is about AFTERNOON storms, not mornings; and no cause is given.

units.title: Reading dense regulation prose fast
units.objective: Strip long official sentences to who / must-may-shall not / what / when, so you can test four choices in about 75–90 seconds.

steps: Mock timing is about 20 items in 25–30 minutes — roughly 75–90 seconds each — and you can't go back. Read the passage once, carefully, rather than skimming it twice.
Strip each sentence to its skeleton: WHO must / may / shall not DO WHAT, WHEN or IF. Skip the padding ('in order to ensure', 'as appropriate', 'in accordance with').
Label the passage's job in two words: a rule, rule + exception, a definition, cause → effect, a contrast. The answer almost always comes from the part your label names.
Then attack the choices one at a time: find the sentence each depends on and check its key word (shall / may, before / after, all / some). Cross out as you go.
Two left? Keep the one you can point to; the other usually needs one assumption you added. The test is adaptive and leaving items blank costs you, so work steadily — but never skip that final check.

worked.passage: In order to ensure the continued airworthiness of naval aircraft, all maintenance actions shall be documented in the maintenance information system at the time the work is performed. Documentation shall be completed by the technician who performed the work and, for any task designated as a mandatory inspection item, verified by a quality assurance representative or a collateral duty inspector. Work that is not documented shall be considered not to have been performed.
worked.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
steps: Skeleton: ALL maintenance documented AT THE TIME of the work. TECHNICIAN documents. QAR or CDI verifies — MANDATORY INSPECTION ITEMS only. NOT DOCUMENTED = NOT DONE.
'Every maintenance action must be verified by a quality assurance representative.' Over-claim — verification is for mandatory inspection items, and a CDI can do it. Out.
'A collateral duty inspector may document work on behalf of the technician.' The technician who did the work completes it. Out.
'Documentation may be completed at the end of the week.' It's 'at the time the work is performed'. Out.
'A repair that was done but never recorded would be treated as if it had not been done.' Straight from the last sentence's skeleton. Proven.
worked.answer: A repair that was carried out but never recorded would be treated as if it had not been performed.

steps: WHO
must / may / shall not
DO WHAT
WHEN / IF / UNLESS

visual.caption: Every regulation sentence shrinks to this skeleton

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Long sentences look scary, but most of the words are padding. Let's throw the padding away.
Cross out openers like 'In order to ensure the continued airworthiness of naval aircraft'. They explain why — the rule comes after.
Now find the rule word: 'shall be documented'.
Find who or what it applies to: 'all maintenance actions'. Find when: 'at the time the work is performed'.
Write the skeleton in five words or so: 'All maintenance logged when done.' Do the same for each sentence.
Now read the choices against your skeletons, not the long passage. A choice that changes WHO, the rule word or WHEN is out.

practice.passage: Keys to ammunition magazines shall be held only by personnel designated in writing by the commanding officer. When not in use, the keys shall be stored in a locked container in a space that is continuously manned.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Any petty officer on watch may hold the magazine keys.
Magazine keys may be stored in an unlocked container if the space is manned.
A space that is left unmanned overnight would not be a suitable place to store the keys.
The commanding officer must carry the magazine keys at all times.
practice.explain: Skeleton: keys stored locked, 'in a space that is continuously manned'. A space unmanned overnight fails that. Keys are held 'only by personnel designated in writing', not any watchstander; the container must be locked AND the space manned; and the CO designates holders rather than carrying the keys.

practice.passage: In order to maintain proficiency, each pilot shall complete a minimum of two instrument approaches, in the simulator or in the aircraft, during every 30-day period. Approaches flown in actual instrument conditions count toward the requirement.
practice.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: Only approaches flown in the aircraft count toward the requirement.
A pilot who flew three approaches in actual instrument conditions during the current 30-day period has met the requirement.
Pilots must fly approaches in actual instrument conditions every 30 days.
Simulator approaches count only when the aircraft is unavailable.
practice.explain: Skeleton: two approaches per 30 days, simulator or aircraft; actual-conditions approaches count. Three counts. Simulator approaches count, so 'only in the aircraft' and 'only when the aircraft is unavailable' fail; and actual conditions COUNT — they are not required.

practice.passage: Hazardous material shall be stored in approved lockers labeled for the class of material they contain, and incompatible materials, such as oxidizers and flammable liquids, shall not be stored in the same locker. A work center may hold no more than one day's supply of any hazardous material outside an approved locker, and that supply shall be returned to the locker at the end of the shift.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Oxidizers and flammable liquids may share a locker that is labeled for both.
A work center may keep a two-day supply outside the locker if it is returned at the end of the shift.
Each work center must keep one day's supply of hazardous material outside the locker.
Hazardous material held outside an approved locker should not still be outside it after the shift ends.
practice.explain: The outside supply 'shall be returned to the locker at the end of the shift'. Incompatible materials 'shall not be stored in the same locker', labels or not; the outside limit is one day's supply; and 'may hold no more than' is a ceiling, not a requirement to hold any.

practice.passage: During emissions control conditions, radars and radio transmitters shall not be operated except as specifically authorized by the tactical action officer. Receivers may continue to be used. Any unauthorized emission shall be reported immediately to the tactical action officer, who will determine whether the ship's position may have been compromised.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: The tactical action officer can permit a particular transmitter to be operated during emissions control.
All electronic equipment must be switched off during emissions control.
Using a receiver during emissions control requires the tactical action officer's authorization.
An unauthorized emission always reveals the ship's position.
practice.explain: Transmitters 'shall not be operated except as specifically authorized by the tactical action officer' — so the TAO can authorize one. 'Receivers may continue to be used', which defeats both the 'all equipment off' and 'receivers need authorization' choices; and the TAO determines whether the position 'may have been' compromised — not 'always'.

practice.passage: Aircraft departing the field shall fly the published departure procedure unless air traffic control has assigned a different procedure. A pilot who cannot comply with an assigned procedure shall advise the controller before takeoff. Noise abatement routes apply to all departures between 2200 and 0700, except departures for an emergency or for a priority mission declared by the operations officer.
practice.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A pilot may fly the published departure even after air traffic control has assigned a different one.
Noise abatement routes apply to departures at any hour of the day.
A pilot who cannot comply with an assigned procedure should tell the controller once airborne.
A departure at 2300 for a priority mission declared by the operations officer could be exempt from the noise abatement route.
practice.explain: Noise routes apply 2200–0700 'except departures for an emergency or for a priority mission declared by the operations officer' — 2300 is in the window, and the exception applies. The published procedure is flown 'unless' ATC assigns another; the routes apply only 2200–0700; and the pilot must advise 'before takeoff'.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's mark up the passage like a checklist: underline, circle, box.
steps: UNDERLINE the rule word in each sentence: shall, may, shall not, must.
CIRCLE the condition or time: if, when, only if, before, after, at the time.
BOX the exception: unless, except, notwithstanding, regardless of.
Cross out everything else — 'in order to ensure…', 'in accordance with…' are padding.
Read the choices against your underlines, circles and boxes only. Any choice that changes one of them is out.
Underline the rule word
Circle the condition
Box the exception
Cross out the padding

example.stem: “In the interest of safety and in accordance with applicable directives, personnel assigned to the flight line shall, prior to the commencement of each shift, conduct an inspection of their assigned tools.” What is the skeleton?
steps: Padding: 'In the interest of safety and in accordance with applicable directives' — cross it out.
Who: personnel assigned to the flight line. Rule word: shall.
When: prior to the commencement of each shift = before each shift. What: inspect their tools.
example.answer: Flight-line personnel shall inspect their tools before each shift.

reteach.hook: Underline, circle, box — and ignore the padding.

check.passage: In order to ensure the integrity of the command's records, personnel shall not remove original service records from the personnel office for any purpose other than transfer to another command, except that a record may be removed temporarily for review by a board when the personnel officer has approved the removal in writing.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: Original service records may be removed from the office for any official purpose.
Original service records may never leave the personnel office.
Boards must review every member's service record.
Review by a board is one of only two purposes for which an original record may leave the office.
check.explain: Skeleton: no removal 'for any purpose other than transfer… except' a board review with written approval — two purposes only. 'Any official purpose' ignores the limit; transfer and board review show records CAN leave; and nothing requires boards to review every record.

check.passage: In order to ensure the integrity of the command's records, personnel shall not remove original service records from the personnel office for any purpose other than transfer to another command, except that a record may be removed temporarily for review by a board when the personnel officer has approved the removal in writing.
check.stem: Based only on the passage, which statement is correct?
options: The passage requires no written approval when an original record leaves the office for a transfer.
The personnel officer may remove records for personal review at any time.
Copies of service records may not be removed from the office.
Records removed for a board need not be returned.
check.explain: The written-approval condition is attached only to the board exception; transfer is permitted with no approval stated. Personal review is not a permitted purpose; copies are never mentioned; and board removal is 'temporarily', so the record comes back.

check.passage: Notwithstanding any other provision of this instruction, an aircraft that has been struck by lightning in flight shall be inspected in accordance with the applicable maintenance manual before further flight, regardless of whether any damage is apparent to the aircrew.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: An aircraft with no visible lightning damage may fly again without an inspection.
The aircrew's report that the aircraft looks undamaged does not remove the inspection requirement.
The aircrew decides whether a lightning inspection is needed.
check.explain: Boxed exception word: inspection is required 'regardless of whether any damage is apparent to the aircrew'. That defeats 'no visible damage' and 'aircrew decides'; and the passage never says strikes always cause damage.

check.passage: Notwithstanding any other provision of this instruction, an aircraft that has been struck by lightning in flight shall be inspected in accordance with the applicable maintenance manual before further flight, regardless of whether any damage is apparent to the aircrew.
check.stem: In the passage, 'notwithstanding any other provision of this instruction' means that this rule —
options: is less important than the rest of the instruction
applies even if another part of the instruction seems to say otherwise
applies only to aircraft without lightning damage
check.explain: 'Notwithstanding' means 'in spite of' — this rule holds whatever else the instruction says. It makes the rule stronger, not weaker; it covers all struck aircraft; and the inspection follows the manual, it doesn't replace it.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Read one sentence at a time.
Ask: WHO is this about?
Ask: what do they have to do (or are allowed to do)?
Ask: WHEN or WHERE?
Say the answers in a few words, like a short note.
Do the same for the next sentence.
Now read the choices and compare them with your notes.
If a choice gets the who, what or when wrong, cross it out.
WHO?
Does WHAT?
WHEN / WHERE?

example.stem: “All hands shall muster on the flight deck at 0700.” Who, what, where and when?
steps: Who: all hands.
What: muster (gather to be counted).
Where: the flight deck. When: 0700.
example.answer: All hands muster on the flight deck at 0700.

reteach.hook: Who, what, when — one sentence at a time.

check.passage: Personnel in the air department shall muster in the hangar bay at 0730. Air department personnel who are on watch at that time will be mustered by their watch supervisors.
check.stem: Based only on the passage, who is to muster in the hangar bay at 0730?
options: only personnel who are on watch
check.explain: Who: 'Personnel in the air department'. The passage never covers everyone aboard, and watch supervisors muster the people on watch rather than being the only ones mustered.

check.passage: Personnel in the air department shall muster in the hangar bay at 0730. Air department personnel who are on watch at that time will be mustered by their watch supervisors.
check.stem: According to the passage, what happens to air department personnel who are on watch at 0730?
options: They leave their watch to muster in the hangar bay.
check.explain: 'Air department personnel who are on watch at that time will be mustered by their watch supervisors.' They are still mustered, not excused, and no later time is given.

check.passage: A fuel sample shall be taken from each aircraft before the first flight of the day. A sample that shows water or sediment shall be reported to maintenance control, and the aircraft shall not fly until the problem has been corrected.
check.stem: Which statement can be inferred only from the passage?
options: A fuel sample is taken after every flight.
Water in a fuel sample is reported to the pilot.
An aircraft whose fuel sample shows water stays on the ground until the problem is fixed.
Sediment in a fuel sample is harmless.
check.explain: The aircraft 'shall not fly until the problem has been corrected'. Samples are taken 'before the first flight of the day', not after every flight; reports go to maintenance control; and sediment is treated as a problem, not harmless.

check.passage: A fuel sample shall be taken from each aircraft before the first flight of the day. A sample that shows water or sediment shall be reported to maintenance control, and the aircraft shall not fly until the problem has been corrected.
check.stem: According to the passage, when is the fuel sample taken?
options: after the last flight of the day
before the first flight of the day
check.explain: When: 'before the first flight of the day'. The other times are never stated.

units.title: Main idea, best title & author's purpose
units.objective: Pick the choice that covers the WHOLE passage — not one detail, not more than the passage says — and name what the writer set out to do.

steps: Main-idea, best-title and primary-purpose questions ask about the passage as a whole. The right answer covers every sentence; each wrong answer covers too little, too much, or something the passage never says.

Find the point before you read the choices. Ask: 'What is this paragraph mainly telling me to do or know?' and say it in one short sentence. In regulation prose the point is usually the rule plus its limits; the other sentences give its reason, conditions, exceptions or procedure.

Too narrow is the most tempting trap: a choice that restates one detail — a time, a distance, one exception. You can point to it in the passage, so it feels proven, but it isn't what the WHOLE passage is about. Watch the first sentence too: on its own it often drops the exception that follows.

Too broad is the other trap: 'naval aviation safety' or 'all shipboard hazards' when the passage covers one procedure. A title should fit like a label on one box, not a label for the whole warehouse. Also reject any choice that adds a claim — always, the most important, prevents all — that the passage never makes.

Purpose questions ask WHY it was written: to require, to define, to correct, to warn, to explain a cause, to set limits. Match the verb to what the passage actually does. Dry procedural paragraphs are almost always written to establish a requirement and its limits — 'to argue', 'to compare' or 'to describe the history of' rarely fit unless the passage really does that.

worked.passage: Each pilot shall conduct a preflight inspection of the assigned aircraft before every flight, using the checklist in the aircraft's flight manual. The inspection does not replace the inspections performed by maintenance personnel; rather, it gives the pilot a final opportunity to detect discrepancies that may have developed since those inspections were completed. Any discrepancy found shall be reported to maintenance control before the aircraft is accepted for flight.
worked.stem: Which choice best expresses the main idea of the passage?
steps: Say the point first: pilots inspect their own aircraft before every flight as a last check on top of maintenance inspections, and report what they find.
'Pilots must report discrepancies to maintenance control.' True — but it's only the last sentence. Too narrow. Out.
'Maintenance inspections are no longer needed because pilots inspect the aircraft.' The passage says the pilot's inspection 'does not replace' them. Contradicted. Out.
'Naval aviation depends on thorough inspections at every level.' Far bigger than one preflight rule, and never stated. Too broad. Out.

'Pilots must inspect their aircraft before each flight as a final check that supplements, rather than replaces, maintenance inspections.' Covers the rule, its purpose and its relationship to maintenance. Keep.
worked.answer: Pilots must inspect their aircraft before each flight as a final check that supplements, rather than replaces, maintenance inspections.

steps: Say the point in one sentence
Too narrow? (one detail)
Too broad? (a bigger topic)
Covers every sentence = answer

visual.caption: The main idea is the label that fits the whole box

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Cover the choices with your hand. Read the passage once.
Ask: if I had to tell a shipmate what this paragraph says in about ten words, what would I say?
Hold that in your head. Here: 'Pilots inspect before every flight as a last check.'
Now uncover the choices. For each one, ask: is this about the WHOLE paragraph, or just one sentence?
Cross out anything about one sentence only, and anything about a much bigger subject than the paragraph.
The one left that matches your ten words is the answer.

practice.passage: During periods of high heat, work centers shall use the wet-bulb globe temperature index to set work and rest cycles for personnel working in exposed areas. As the index rises, the permitted work period shortens and the required rest period lengthens. Supervisors shall ensure that drinking water is available at every work site and that personnel showing signs of heat illness are removed from work and evaluated by medical.
practice.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Drinking water must be available at every work site.
Personnel working in high heat are entitled to longer rest periods than work periods.
Heat limits work by a measured index, and supervisors must guard against heat illness.
Heat illness is the most serious hazard faced by personnel who work in exposed areas aboard ship.
practice.explain: Every sentence fits under it: the index sets work and rest, and supervisors provide water and remove anyone showing heat illness. Drinking water is one detail (too narrow); rest only lengthens as the index rises — the passage never says rest exceeds work; and nothing ranks heat illness against other hazards.

practice.passage: Wheel chocks shall be installed on every parked aircraft. Chocks shall be removed only on a signal from the plane captain or director, and only after the pilot has confirmed that the brakes are set. On the flight deck, tie-down chains shall be installed in addition to chocks whenever the aircraft is not about to taxi.
practice.stem: Which of the following would be the best title for the passage?
options: Securing Parked Aircraft with Chocks and Tie-Downs
The Duties of the Plane Captain
Confirming Brakes Are Set Before Chocks Are Removed
practice.explain: The passage covers installing chocks, the conditions for removing them and adding tie-down chains on the flight deck — all ways of securing parked aircraft. The plane captain appears only as one of two people who signal; 'Flight Deck Safety' is far broader (and the chock rule applies everywhere); and the brake check is one condition inside one sentence.

practice.passage: The deck log is the official chronological record of events affecting the ship, her crew and her operations. Entries shall be made in ink by the officer of the deck or a designated assistant, and errors shall be corrected by a single line through the incorrect entry, initialed by the person making the correction. No page shall be removed from the log for any reason.
practice.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to —
options: explain why the deck log is more important than any other record kept by the ship
describe the deck log and set rules that protect the integrity of its entries
list the events that must be recorded in the deck log
assign responsibility for reviewing the deck log to the officer of the deck
practice.explain: Sentence 1 says what the deck log is; the rest set rules — ink, single-line corrections with initials, no pages removed — that keep the record trustworthy. No other record is compared; no list of events is given; and the officer of the deck MAKES entries — reviewing the log is never mentioned.

practice.passage: Intentional spins are prohibited in all squadron aircraft except during the spin-training phase of the syllabus. During that phase, spins shall be entered only above 10,000 feet above ground level, only in designated working areas, and only with an instructor pilot at the controls or in the other seat. Students shall not practice spins on solo flights under any circumstances.
practice.stem: Which choice best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Spins are the most dangerous maneuver taught in the syllabus.
Intentional spins are prohibited in all squadron aircraft.
Spin training must be conducted above 10,000 feet in designated working areas.
Spins are allowed only in spin training, and then only within strict limits.
practice.explain: The passage bans spins, carves out the training phase, and fences that exception with altitude, area, instructor and no-solo limits. The first sentence alone drops its own 'except' clause — the classic topic-sentence trap; the 10,000-foot rule is one detail; and no maneuver is ranked as most dangerous.

practice.passage: Aircrew shall be provided an opportunity for at least eight hours of uninterrupted sleep in every 24-hour period. Rest begins when the member is released from all duties, not when the last flight lands, so time spent on debriefs and paperwork counts against the rest period rather than toward it. Schedules that cannot meet this standard shall be approved in advance by the commanding officer.
practice.stem: Which of the following would be the best title for the passage?
options: Minimum Sleep Requirements for All Squadron Personnel
Minimum Crew Rest and When It Begins
Commanding Officer Approval of Flight Schedules
practice.explain: The passage sets an eight-hour minimum for aircrew, explains when the rest period starts counting, and says who approves schedules that fall short — a minimum and how it is measured. 'All squadron personnel' widens 'aircrew' (scope shift); CO approval covers only schedules that can't meet the standard (too narrow); and mishaps are never mentioned (outside knowledge).

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's use the umbrella test — the main idea is the umbrella that every sentence fits under.
steps: Number the sentences. Next to each number, write two or three words for its job: 'rule', 'reason', 'exception', 'how to report'.
Look for the umbrella: the one idea that all your numbered jobs serve. In a regulation, it's usually the rule together with its limits.
Hold each choice over the sentences. Does every sentence fit under it? If one sentence sticks out, the umbrella is too small — too narrow.
If the umbrella also covers things the passage never mentions — other procedures, all of naval aviation — it's too big. Out as well.
A title takes the same test in fewer words. For a purpose question, name what the passage DOES (requires, defines, corrects, warns) and match that verb.
Number the sentences
Label each one's job
Find the idea they all serve
Umbrella too small or too big? Out

example.stem: “Watertight doors marked for Condition Zebra shall be closed when the ship sets Condition Zebra. They may be opened only with the damage control assistant's permission, and they shall be closed again immediately after passage.” Which is the main idea: (a) Zebra doors need permission to be opened, or (b) Zebra doors stay closed during Condition Zebra except for brief, approved passage?
steps: (a) covers part of sentence 2 only — the closing rule and the 'close again' requirement are left out. Umbrella too small.
(b) covers the closing rule, the permission exception and the 'closed again immediately' requirement. Every sentence fits under it.

reteach.hook: The main idea is the umbrella every sentence fits under — no bigger, no smaller.

check.passage: All transmissions on the command's tactical circuits shall be recorded in the radio log, including the time, the station calling and a summary of the message. Operators shall not make personal or unofficial transmissions on these circuits. The communications officer shall review the log daily and report any violation of circuit discipline to the executive officer.
check.stem: Which choice best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: The communications officer is responsible for disciplining operators throughout the command.
Tactical circuits must be logged, kept to official traffic and reviewed for violations.
Personal transmissions are prohibited on tactical circuits.
The radio log records the time of each transmission.
check.explain: Sentence 1 (log everything), sentence 2 (official traffic only) and sentence 3 (daily review for violations) all fit under it. The communications officer reviews and REPORTS violations — disciplining operators is never mentioned; the other two choices are single details.

check.passage: All transmissions on the command's tactical circuits shall be recorded in the radio log, including the time, the station calling and a summary of the message. Operators shall not make personal or unofficial transmissions on these circuits. The communications officer shall review the log daily and report any violation of circuit discipline to the executive officer.
check.stem: The primary purpose of the passage is to —
options: set rules for recording and using the command's tactical circuits
explain how an adversary can intercept radio transmissions
describe how the executive officer punishes violations of circuit discipline
compare tactical circuits with unofficial circuits
check.explain: Every sentence is a 'shall' rule about logging, using or reviewing the circuits. Interception is outside knowledge; the executive officer only receives reports — punishment is never described; and no comparison is made.

check.passage: The quarterdeck watch shall verify the identification of every person who boards the ship in port. Visitors shall be logged aboard, escorted at all times while aboard and logged ashore when they depart. Any person who cannot produce valid identification shall be denied access and reported to the officer of the deck.
check.stem: Which of the following would be the best title for the passage?
options: Shipboard Security at Sea and in Port
Duties of the Officer of the Deck in Port
Controlling Access to the Ship in Port
check.explain: Verifying identification, logging and escorting visitors, and turning away people without ID are all ways of controlling who comes aboard in port. The passage covers only port, not sea (too broad); the OOD only receives reports; and escorting is one detail (too narrow).

check.passage: The quarterdeck watch shall verify the identification of every person who boards the ship in port. Visitors shall be logged aboard, escorted at all times while aboard and logged ashore when they depart. Any person who cannot produce valid identification shall be denied access and reported to the officer of the deck.
check.stem: Which choice best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Visitors may not board the ship in port.
The quarterdeck watch is responsible for the safety of all visitors while they are aboard.
Everyone boarding in port is identified, and visitors are tracked and escorted.
Persons without valid identification are reported to the officer of the deck.
check.explain: It sums up the passage: everyone is identified (and anyone who can't be is turned away), and visitors are logged and escorted. Visitors CAN board — they are logged and escorted; the watch verifies identification, but the passage never makes it responsible for visitors' safety; and the report to the OOD is one detail.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: A paragraph is about ONE main thing.
The main idea is what the whole paragraph is about — not just one sentence.
A detail is one small fact inside the paragraph: a time, a number, a name.
Details are true, but a detail is not the main idea.
A good title is the main idea said in a few words.
The purpose is WHY someone wrote it: to give a rule, to explain something, to warn you.
If a choice is about just one sentence, it's too small.
If a choice is about much more than the paragraph, it's too big.
Too small: one detail
Just right: the whole paragraph
Too big: more than the paragraph

example.stem: “Sailors shall wear safety shoes in the hangar. The shoes shall have steel toes. Worn-out shoes shall be replaced.” Which is the main idea: (a) safety shoes must have steel toes, (b) rules for safety shoes in the hangar, or (c) all the safety equipment used aboard ship?
steps: (a) is one detail — sentence 2 only. Too small.
(c) is much more than the paragraph talks about. Too big.
(b) covers all three sentences. Just right.
example.answer: (b) Rules for safety shoes in the hangar.

reteach.hook: Not too small, not too big — the whole paragraph.

check.passage: Only designated mail clerks may enter the ship's post office. Mail shall be sorted and delivered on the day it arrives aboard. Registered mail shall be signed for by the person to whom it is addressed.
check.stem: Which of the following would be the best title for the passage?
options: The History of the Navy Mail Service
check.explain: All three sentences are about the ship's mail: who enters the post office, when mail is delivered and how registered mail is signed for. Registered mail is one detail; history is never mentioned; and 'administrative procedures' is far bigger than mail.

check.passage: Only designated mail clerks may enter the ship's post office. Mail shall be sorted and delivered on the day it arrives aboard. Registered mail shall be signed for by the person to whom it is addressed.
check.stem: The passage was mainly written to —
options: give the rules for handling the ship's mail
explain why mail is so important to the crew's morale
warn that mail is often lost aboard ship
describe how mail clerks are trained
check.explain: Each sentence is a rule about mail. Morale, lost mail and training may sound sensible, but the passage never mentions them.

check.passage: Personnel shall face the ladder when climbing up or down. They shall keep one hand on the handrail at all times. Tools and equipment shall be raised or lowered by line rather than carried by hand on the ladder.
check.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Tools must be raised and lowered by line.
Ladders are the most dangerous places aboard ship.
The passage gives rules for using ladders safely.
Personnel must never climb ladders while carrying anything.
check.explain: Facing the ladder, keeping a hand on the rail and using a line for tools are all ladder-safety rules. The tool rule is one detail; nothing compares ladders with other places; and the passage bans carrying TOOLS AND EQUIPMENT by hand — it never says 'anything', and it never says 'never climb'.

check.passage: Personnel shall face the ladder when climbing up or down. They shall keep one hand on the handrail at all times. Tools and equipment shall be raised or lowered by line rather than carried by hand on the ladder.
check.stem: The passage was mainly written to —
options: compare ladders with other ways of moving between decks
explain how shipboard ladders are built
praise sailors who climb ladders safely
tell personnel how to use ladders safely
check.explain: Every sentence is an instruction for using a ladder. No comparison, construction details or praise appear in the passage.

units.title: Word meaning, qualifiers & paragraph structure
units.objective: Work out what a word means HERE, read exactly what a qualifier allows, and see how a paragraph is built — so you can name the job of every sentence.

steps: Word-in-context questions ask what a word means IN THIS PASSAGE. The trap answer is the word's most common everyday meaning. Navy prose uses many words in a special sense: to 'secure' a radar is to shut it off; a watchstander who is 'relieved' has been replaced; an 'evolution' is a planned operation.

Method: cover the word, read its sentence and the next one, and put in your own replacement. Pick the choice closest to your replacement, then plug it back in — the sentence must keep the same meaning.

Qualifiers set how strong a statement is: shall / may, all / most / some, always / normally / seldom, only / at least / no more than. A qualifier question asks what the word allows and what it rules out. 'At least 30 minutes' allows 45; 'no more than two' allows none; 'normally' admits exceptions.

Transition words show how sentences connect. Contrast: however, but, although, nevertheless. Result: therefore, consequently, accordingly, for this reason. Adding: also, in addition, further. Example: for example, such as. Exception: unless, except. The transition tells you the job of the sentence it starts.

Paragraph structure: regulation paragraphs follow a few patterns — rule → reason; rule → exception → limit on the exception; definition → requirement; problem → cause → remedy. Give each sentence a one-word job (rule, reason, definition, exception, procedure) before reading the choices; your list of jobs IS the organization.

worked.passage: Before personnel go aloft or work near an antenna, the radars and transmitters that could endanger them shall be secured, and a danger tag shall be hung at each control station. The equipment shall remain secured until all personnel have reported clear of the area, and only then may it be restored to operation.
worked.stem: As used in the passage, the word 'secured' most nearly means —
steps: Everyday meaning of 'secured': fastened down, or protected from theft. That's the trap.
Cover the word: radars that 'could endanger them' shall be ___ before people go aloft. What removes the danger from a radar? Switching it off.
Check the next clue: the equipment stays ___ until personnel are clear, 'and only then may it be restored to operation'. Restored to operation = switched back on, so ___ = switched off.
'Locked in place' and 'guarded against intruders' fit the everyday sense but do nothing about radiation; 'inspected' doesn't stop a radar transmitting. Out.
worked.answer: shut down (switched off)

steps: Cover the word
Put in your own word
Pick the closest choice
Plug it back in — same meaning?

visual.caption: The passage defines the word, not the dictionary

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Find the word the question asks about and put your finger over it.
Read the whole sentence, and the sentence after it, with the word hidden.
Ask: what simple word would make sense in the gap? Say it in your head.
Here: radars must be '___' so they don't hurt people aloft, and afterward they are 'restored to operation'. The gap must mean 'turned off'.
Now look at the choices. Pick the one that means the same as your word.
Put that choice into the sentence. If the sentence still makes sense and means the same thing, you're done.

practice.passage: Liberty for the duty section ends at 2200. Liberty for non-duty sections expires at 0700 the following morning, although the commanding officer may, at his or her discretion, grant extended liberty for holidays or after a long deployment. Members who return late shall report to the officer of the deck.
practice.stem: As used in the passage, the phrase 'at his or her discretion' most nearly means —
options: according to his or her own judgment
only with the approval of higher authority
practice.explain: The CO 'may' grant extended liberty for holidays or after deployment — a choice left to the CO's judgment. 'In secret' confuses 'discretion' with being 'discreet'; needing higher approval would take the choice away from the CO; and 'may… for holidays or after a long deployment' describes occasional decisions, not a fixed schedule.

practice.passage: Anti-exposure suits shall be worn on overwater flights when the water temperature is below 50°F. When the water temperature is from 50°F to 60°F, the commanding officer may waive the requirement after weighing the risk of cold-water immersion against the risk of heat stress in the cockpit. However, no waiver may be granted when the outside air temperature is also below 32°F.
practice.stem: The word 'However' at the start of the last sentence signals that the sentence —
options: gives an example of a situation in which the waiver in the second sentence applies
states the result of granting a waiver
places a limit on the waiver authority described in the second sentence
repeats the requirement stated in the first sentence
practice.explain: 'However' is a contrast word: the second sentence lets the CO waive the suit at 50–60°F, and the last sentence says no waiver when the air is also below 32°F — a limit on that authority. It gives no example, no result of a waiver, and it doesn't restate the below-50°F rule.

practice.passage: Portable fire extinguishers shall be inspected at least once a month and after each use. An extinguisher that has been partially discharged shall be removed from service and recharged, even if its gauge still shows pressure in the operating range. Inspection dates shall be recorded on the tag attached to each extinguisher.
practice.stem: Based on the passage, the words 'at least once a month' mean that an extinguisher —
options: must be inspected exactly once each month
may go two months between inspections if it has not been used
must be inspected only after it has been used
may be inspected more than once in a month
practice.explain: 'At least once' sets a floor, not a ceiling — more often is allowed, and the 'after each use' rule can add inspections. 'Exactly once' turns the floor into a fixed number; two months without inspection falls below the floor; and use is an extra trigger, not the only one.

practice.passage: Foreign object damage is any damage to an aircraft or engine caused by an object that does not belong in it, such as a loose bolt, a rag or a stone. Because a single small object drawn into an engine intake can destroy the engine, every person working on the flight line shall inspect the area around the aircraft before engines are started. Tools shall also be inventoried at the end of each task so that a missing tool can be found before the aircraft flies.
practice.stem: Which choice best describes how the passage is organized?
options: A term is defined, its danger justifies a requirement, and another requirement is added.
A problem is described, and several of its possible causes are compared.
A general rule is stated, and exceptions to it are then listed.
A requirement is stated first, and the term that the requirement uses is defined afterward.
practice.explain: Sentence jobs: definition (foreign object damage) → reason + requirement ('Because… shall inspect') → added requirement ('also… inventoried'). Examples like bolts and rags illustrate the term — no causes are compared; there are no exceptions; and the definition comes FIRST, so the last choice reverses the order.

practice.passage: Normal procedures shall be performed from the checklist, not from memory. Experience has shown that crews who rely on memory are most likely to omit a step when they are interrupted or under time pressure, which are exactly the conditions in which an omission is most dangerous. Emergency procedures marked as memory items are an exception: they shall be performed immediately from memory and then confirmed against the checklist once the aircraft is under control.
practice.stem: What is the main function of the second sentence in the passage?
options: It gives an exception to the rule stated in the first sentence.
It explains the reason for the rule stated in the first sentence.
It identifies which procedures are to be performed from memory.
It describes what happens to an aircraft when a step is omitted in an emergency.
practice.explain: Sentence 1 is the rule (use the checklist); sentence 2 explains why — memory fails under interruption and time pressure, when omissions matter most. The exception and the memory items both belong to sentence 3, and sentence 2 says omissions are 'most dangerous' without describing what happens to the aircraft.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's treat every small word as a signpost — it tells you where the sentence is going.
steps: For a word-meaning question, ignore what the word 'usually' means. Find two clues in the passage — what the word does and what undoes it — and let them define it.
For a qualifier, draw its fence: 'at least 30' = 30 or more; 'no more than 2' = 0, 1 or 2; 'normally' = usually, exceptions possible; 'only if' = a must-have condition.

For a transition, drop it into a bin: CONTRAST (however, but, although, nevertheless), RESULT (therefore, consequently, accordingly), ADD (also, in addition, further), EXAMPLE (for example, such as), EXCEPTION (unless, except).
For structure, give every sentence a one-word job — rule, reason, definition, exception, example, procedure, result — and read your job list top to bottom. That list IS the organization.
Match each choice to your fence, bin or job list. A choice that names the wrong bin, the wrong job or the wrong order is out.
Contrast: however, although
Result: therefore, accordingly
Add: also, in addition
Exception: unless, except
