40 cm behind the lens; real, inverted, two-thirds size
practice.explain: 1/d_i = 1/20 − 1/60 = 3/60 − 1/60 = 2/60, so d_i = 30 cm on the far side. Magnification = 30 ÷ 60 = 0.5. The object is beyond 2F (40 cm), so the image is real, inverted and smaller. 15 cm adds the reciprocals instead of subtracting; 40 cm just subtracts the distances.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's sort every optics question with two quick questions: does it bring light together or spread it out, and where is the object?
steps: Bringers-together (converging): a convex lens, fat in the middle, and a concave mirror, caved in like the bowl of a spoon.
Spreaders (diverging): a concave lens, thin in the middle, and a convex mirror, bulging like the back of a spoon.
Spreaders are easy: always smaller, upright and virtual.
Bringers-together: a far-off object gives a small, upside-down, real image; an object inside the focal point gives a big, upright, virtual one.
Real images are always upside down and can land on a screen. Virtual images are upright and cannot.
Bending: into glass or water, light slows and bends toward the normal; out again, it speeds up and bends away.
Converging: convex lens, concave mirror
Diverging: concave lens, convex mirror
Diverging: always small, upright, virtual

example.stem: You look into the bowl of a shiny spoon held at arm's length. What kind of mirror is it, and what do you see?
steps: The bowl curves inward: a concave (converging) mirror.
Your face is far beyond its tiny focal length.
So the image is real, smaller and upside down.
example.answer: A concave mirror; a small, upside-down image

reteach.hook: Fat lens or caved-in mirror: converge. Real means upside down.

check.stem: Which of these ALWAYS produces a smaller, upright, virtual image, wherever the object is?
check.explain: Diverging optics (concave lens, convex mirror) can only spread light, so they always give a smaller, upright, virtual image. A flat mirror's image is the same size. Converging optics change their image with the object's distance.

check.stem: A slide projector throws a large, sharp picture onto a screen. The image on the screen is —
options: virtual and inverted, so it needs a mirror to flip it
real and inverted, so slides go in upside down
check.explain: Only a real image can fall on a screen, and real images are inverted, which is why slides are loaded upside down. A virtual image cannot be projected at all.

check.stem: A swimming pool looks shallower than it really is. This is caused by —
options: reflection off the bottom of the pool
the water magnifying the bottom like a lens
light slowing down as it enters the water
refraction as light leaves the water
check.explain: Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water into air. Your eye traces it back in a straight line to a point higher than the real bottom. The light that matters is coming OUT of the water, not going in.

check.stem: A ray of light hits a flat mirror at 20° to the mirror's surface. What is its angle of reflection, measured from the normal?
check.explain: The normal is at 90° to the surface, so the angle of incidence is 90 − 20 = 70°, and the angle of reflection equals it: 70°. 20° measures from the surface, not the normal; 40° and 140° are angles between the two rays.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and build it from the ground up. One small step at a time.
steps: Light travels in straight lines until it hits something.
A mirror bounces light: it leaves at the same angle it arrived.
Light bends when it goes from air into water or glass. That bending is called refraction.
A lens that is fatter in the middle brings light together at a point called the focal point.
A lens that is thinner in the middle spreads light out.
Your reflection in a flat mirror is the right way up, the same size, and seems to be behind the glass.
Light hits the mirror
Same angle out as in
Image seems to be behind the glass

example.stem: Light hits a mirror at 40° from the normal. At what angle does it bounce off?
steps: Angle in equals angle out.
Both are measured from the normal, the line straight out from the mirror.
So it leaves at 40° on the other side of the normal.

reteach.hook: Angle in = angle out. A fat lens brings light together.

check.stem: A pencil standing in a glass of water looks bent at the water's surface. Why?
options: Light bends as it passes from water into air
The water magnifies only the bottom half
The glass reflects the light back
The pencil really does bend slightly under water
check.explain: Light from the underwater part bends as it leaves the water (refraction), so that part appears in a slightly different place and the pencil looks broken at the surface.

check.stem: A lens that is thicker in the middle than at its edges is a —
check.explain: Thicker in the middle means convex, and a convex lens converges light to a focal point. Concave lenses are thinner in the middle and spread light out.

check.stem: You stand 2 m in front of a flat mirror. How far from you does your image appear to be?
options: 0 m, because it is on the glass
check.explain: The image appears as far behind the mirror as you are in front of it: 2 m behind. So it is 2 + 2 = 4 m from you. 2 m is the distance to the mirror, not to the image.

check.stem: Light hits a mirror at 30° from the normal. At what angle from the normal does it reflect?
check.explain: Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 30°. 60° is the angle to the mirror's surface instead of the normal.

astb-anit.title: Aviation & Nautical Information
astb-anit.blurb: How aircraft fly and are operated, plus ships, rules of the road, carrier ops and naval aviation history. A knowledge test: about two-thirds aviation, one-third nautical, and every fact here is fair game.

units.title: Aircraft, controls & aerodynamics
units.objective: Name each control surface and the axis it works on, and explain lift, stalls, load factor, adverse yaw and wake turbulence.

steps: Three axes all pass through the center of gravity. Longitudinal (nose to tail): ROLL, controlled by the ailerons. Lateral (wingtip to wingtip): PITCH, controlled by the elevator or stabilator. Vertical: YAW, controlled by the rudder.

Combined surfaces: elevons (elevator + aileron, on delta wings), ruddervators (rudder + elevator, on V-tails), flaperons (flap + aileron). A stabilator is a one-piece moving tail; its antiservo tab moves the SAME way as its trailing edge.
A trim tab moves OPPOSITE to its surface and holds it in place. Tab down pushes the elevator up, which holds the nose up.

Four forces: lift opposes weight and thrust opposes drag. In steady, unaccelerated flight each pair is equal. Angle of attack (AOA) is the angle between the chord line and the relative wind. Past the critical AOA the wing stalls, at any airspeed or attitude.

Adverse yaw: the lowered aileron makes more lift AND more induced drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn. Fixes: coordinated rudder, differential ailerons (the up aileron travels farther) and Frise ailerons (the raised aileron's nose pokes into the airflow).

In a level turn, load factor = 1 ÷ cos(bank): 60° gives 2 G, and stall speed rises by √2 (about 41%). Wake vortices are strongest behind aircraft that are heavy, clean and slow. Ground effect, within about one wingspan of the surface, cuts induced drag.
teach.formula: Ailerons → roll (longitudinal) · Elevator → pitch (lateral) · Rudder → yaw (vertical) · Load factor = 1 ÷ cos(bank)

worked.stem: An airplane stalls at 60 knots in wings-level flight. At about what speed will it stall in a level 60°-bank turn?
steps: Load factor in a level turn = 1 ÷ cos(bank). cos 60° = 0.5, so the load factor is 2 G.
Stall speed rises with the SQUARE ROOT of load factor: √2 ≈ 1.41.
The trap is doubling the speed to 120 knots. Load factor doubles; stall speed goes up by only about 41%.
worked.answer: About 85 knots

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Picture an airplane with three skewers stuck through its middle.
One skewer runs nose to tail. Rocking the wings around it is ROLL, and the ailerons on the wingtips do it.
One skewer runs wingtip to wingtip. Nodding the nose up and down around it is PITCH, and the elevator on the tail does it.
One skewer runs straight up and down. Swinging the nose left and right around it is YAW, and the rudder on the tail fin does it.
A wing lifts best when it meets the air at a slight angle. Tip it up too far and the air stops flowing smoothly over the top. That's a stall, and it's about the angle, not the speed.
In a steep turn the wing has to lift more than the airplane's weight, so it stalls at a higher speed than usual.
Ailerons: roll
Elevator: pitch
Rudder: yaw
Trim tab: opposite its surface

visual.caption: Each surface and the motion it controls

practice.stem: Which control surface rolls an airplane about its longitudinal axis?
practice.explain: Ailerons work in opposite directions on the two wings, so one wing rises while the other drops: roll about the nose-to-tail axis. The elevator pitches and the rudder yaws.

practice.stem: The angle of attack is the angle between the wing's chord line and the —
practice.explain: AOA is measured from the chord line to the relative wind. The angle between the chord line and the longitudinal axis is the angle of incidence, a fixed design angle.

practice.stem: On a V-tail airplane, the surfaces that do the jobs of both rudder and elevator are called —
practice.explain: Ruddervator = rudder + elevator. Elevons combine elevator and ailerons; flaperons combine flaps and ailerons; a stabilator is a one-piece moving horizontal tail.

practice.stem: A pilot rolls left using ailerons alone. Which way does adverse yaw push the nose?
options: It doesn't; ailerons cause no yaw
practice.explain: The rising right wing has the lowered aileron, which adds lift and induced drag. That extra drag pulls the right wing back and yaws the nose right, opposite the turn.

practice.stem: A pilot trims for a nose-down attitude in cruise. Which describes the elevator trim tab?
options: Tab moves down, holding the elevator up
Tab moves down, holding the elevator down
Tab moves up, holding the elevator down
Tab moves up, holding the elevator up
practice.explain: Nose-down needs the elevator held DOWN. A trim tab moves opposite to its surface, so the tab goes UP and the air pressure on it pushes the elevator down.

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's sort the controls and devices by the problem each one solves.
steps: Problem: point the airplane. Ailerons roll it about the longitudinal axis, the elevator pitches it about the lateral axis, and the rudder yaws it about the vertical axis.
Problem: tired arms. Trim tabs hold a surface in place, moving OPPOSITE to it. The exception is the stabilator's antiservo tab, which moves WITH its trailing edge to add feel.
Problem: flying slowly. Flaps add camber (Fowler flaps add wing area too), and slots and slats let the wing reach a higher angle of attack before stalling.
Problem: coming down or rolling fast. Spoilers kill lift on their wing, so that wing drops.
Problem: adverse yaw. The down aileron's extra drag yaws the nose away from the turn. Coordinated rudder, differential ailerons or Frise ailerons cancel it.
Problem: stalling in a turn. Load factor = 1 ÷ cos(bank) and stall speed rises by its square root. 45° gives 1.41 G, 60° gives 2 G.
Point it: the three controls
Hold it: trim tabs
Fly slow: flaps, slats
Dump lift: spoilers

visual.caption: Every device solves a problem

example.stem: Which device lets a wing reach a higher angle of attack before it stalls: flaps, spoilers, slats or trim tabs?
steps: Spoilers destroy lift, the opposite of what we want.
Trim tabs only relieve control pressure.
Slats open a gap that feeds fast air over the top of the wing, delaying the stall to a higher angle of attack.

reteach.hook: Ailerons roll, elevator pitches, rudder yaws; trim moves opposite.

check.stem: Rotation about the vertical axis is called —
check.explain: Yaw is the nose swinging left or right about the vertical axis, controlled by the rudder.

check.stem: A Fowler flap differs from a plain flap because it —
options: is mounted on the leading edge
check.explain: The Fowler flap moves back on tracks as well as down, so it adds wing area and camber, giving the largest lift increase.

check.stem: In a level 45°-bank turn, the load factor is about —
check.explain: 1 ÷ cos 45° = 1 ÷ 0.707 ≈ 1.41 G. 2 G is the figure for 60°.

check.stem: Behind which aircraft would you expect the strongest wake turbulence?
options: A light airplane, fast, flaps down
A heavy jet, slow, gear and flaps up
A heavy jet, fast, gear and flaps down
A light airplane, slow, gear up
check.explain: The strongest vortices come from heavy, clean, slow aircraft, which fly at a high angle of attack.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down. One part of the airplane at a time.
steps: The wings make lift. The fuselage is the body. The tail (empennage) keeps the airplane steady.
Ailerons are hinged flaps near the wingtips. One goes up while the other goes down, so the airplane rolls.
The elevator is the hinged part of the flat tail. Tilt it and the nose goes up or down.
The rudder is the hinged part of the upright tail fin. It swings the nose left or right.
Four forces act on every airplane: lift pulls up, weight pulls down, thrust pulls forward, drag pulls back.
If the wing is tilted too steeply into the air, it stalls and loses its lift.
Lift: up
Weight: down
Thrust: forward
Drag: back

visual.caption: The four forces

example.stem: Which force does the engine and propeller produce?
steps: The propeller pulls the airplane forward through the air.
The forward force is called thrust.

reteach.hook: Lift beats weight, thrust beats drag.

check.stem: Which part of the airplane makes most of the lift?
check.explain: The wings are airfoils shaped to make lift as air flows over them.

check.stem: The force that holds an airplane back is —
check.explain: Drag is air resistance acting against the airplane's motion. Thrust opposes it.

check.stem: The rudder is found on the —
check.explain: The rudder hinges on the vertical stabilizer (tail fin) and yaws the nose left or right.

check.stem: A wing stalls when it —
options: meets the air at too steep an angle
check.explain: A stall happens when the angle of attack exceeds the critical angle and the airflow breaks away from the top of the wing.

units.title: Engines & flight instruments
units.objective: Explain the four-stroke cycle, carburetor ice, mixture and turbine engines, and know what each instrument senses and how it fails.

steps: Four-stroke cycle: intake, compression, power, exhaust. Each stroke is half a crankshaft turn, so one cycle takes two revolutions. The spark fires near the end of the compression stroke, and two engine-driven magnetos keep it firing even if the electrical system dies.

Carburetor ice forms in the venturi from fuel evaporation and pressure drop, most often below about 70°F in humid air. First sign: lost RPM with a fixed-pitch prop, or lower manifold pressure with a constant-speed prop. Carb heat richens the mixture, because warm air is less dense.

Higher altitude means thinner air, so the mixture gets too rich: lean it. Fuel of too low a grade causes detonation, an explosive burn of the charge. Preignition is the charge lighting early from a hot spot.

Gas turbines: intake → compressor → combustor → turbine → exhaust. The turbine drives the compressor. A turbofan's bypass ratio is the air going AROUND the core divided by the air going THROUGH it. Turboprops drive propellers and turboshafts drive rotors. Afterburners burn extra fuel behind the turbine.

Pitot-static instruments: the airspeed indicator uses pitot AND static pressure; the altimeter and VSI use static only. A blocked static port freezes the altimeter and zeroes the VSI. With the pitot inlet and drain hole both blocked, the ASI reads like an altimeter and shows more speed as you climb.

Gyros: the attitude and heading indicators use rigidity in space; the turn coordinator uses precession. Altimetry: pressure altitude is read with 29.92 set, and density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for temperature. 'High to low, look out below': flying into lower pressure or colder air puts you lower than indicated.
teach.formula: Intake → Compression → Power → Exhaust · ASI = pitot + static · Altimeter & VSI = static · 1 in Hg ≈ 1,000 ft

worked.stem: A pilot departs with 30.15 set and flies to an area where the altimeter setting is 29.65, without resetting. The altimeter reads 4,500 feet. About how high is the airplane really?
steps: The pressure has dropped by 30.15 − 29.65 = 0.50 in Hg. At about 1,000 feet per inch, that is a 500-foot error.
With too HIGH a setting, the altimeter over-reads: 'high to low, look out below'.
Setting the correct 29.65 would drop the reading by about 500 feet.
True altitude ≈ 4,500 − 500 = 4,000 feet.
worked.answer: About 4,000 feet, 500 feet lower than indicated

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: A piston engine breathes in four steps. Remember 'suck, squeeze, bang, blow'.
SUCK (intake): the piston goes down and pulls in fuel and air.
SQUEEZE (compression): the piston comes up and squashes the mixture.
BANG (power): the spark plug fires, the mixture burns and shoves the piston down. This is the only step that makes power.
BLOW (exhaust): the piston comes up and pushes the burnt gas out.
Instruments: the altimeter is really a barometer. Air pressure falls as you climb, and the altimeter turns that pressure into feet.

visual.caption: The power stroke: spark fires, both valves closed

practice.stem: Which is the correct order of the four strokes?
practice.explain: Intake draws the charge in, compression squeezes it, the power stroke burns it, and exhaust clears it out. 'Suck, squeeze, bang, blow.'

practice.stem: Which instrument uses static pressure only?
practice.explain: The altimeter (and the VSI) work from static pressure alone. The airspeed indicator also needs pitot pressure; the attitude indicator and turn coordinator are gyros.

practice.stem: Pressure altitude is the altitude shown when the altimeter is set to —
practice.explain: Pressure altitude is referenced to the standard datum, 29.92 in Hg (1013.2 hPa). Correct it for nonstandard temperature to get density altitude.

practice.stem: In a turbojet, what drives the compressor?
practice.explain: Hot gas from the combustor spins the turbine, which turns the compressor through a shared shaft. The afterburner only adds thrust behind the turbine.

practice.stem: A pilot of a fixed-pitch-propeller airplane notices RPM slowly falling in cool, humid air and applies carburetor heat. If ice is present, the pilot should expect RPM to —
options: rise at once and stay high
drop at first, then rise as the ice melts
practice.explain: Warm air is less dense, so carb heat first richens the mixture and costs a little RPM. As the ice melts the airflow is restored and RPM rises (FAA PHAK).

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's ask what each instrument is actually measuring.
steps: The altimeter measures static (outside) air pressure and shows it as height. Lower pressure reads higher.
The VSI measures how FAST the static pressure is changing, so it shows a climb or descent rate.
The airspeed indicator compares pitot (ram) pressure with static pressure. It needs BOTH.
So if static is blocked, all three are affected: the altimeter freezes, the VSI reads zero and the ASI is wrong. If only the pitot is blocked, only the ASI is wrong.
The gyros measure motion, not air. The attitude and heading indicators hold their position (rigidity in space); the turn coordinator senses the gyro being pushed (precession).
Altimeter errors: too high a setting, or air colder than standard, means you are LOWER than you think. 'High to low (or hot to cold), look out below.'
Static only: altimeter, VSI
Pitot + static: airspeed
Rigidity: attitude, heading
Precession: turn coordinator

visual.caption: What each instrument senses

example.stem: Ice blocks the static port in level flight. The pilot then descends. What do the altimeter and VSI show?
steps: With the static port blocked, the static pressure stays at the level-flight value.
The altimeter keeps showing that same altitude: it is frozen.
The VSI sees no change in pressure, so it reads zero.

reteach.hook: Static feeds three; pitot feeds one; gyros feel motion.

check.stem: If only the pitot tube is blocked, which instrument is affected?
check.explain: Only the airspeed indicator uses pitot pressure. The altimeter and VSI use static only.

check.stem: Density altitude is —
options: pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature
altitude read with the local setting
check.explain: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for temperature; it governs aircraft performance. Height above the ground is absolute altitude.

check.stem: Applying carburetor heat makes the mixture —
check.explain: Warm air is less dense, so the same fuel meets less air and the mixture richens, slightly lowering power.

check.stem: A turbofan with a high bypass ratio gets most of its thrust from —
options: the fan air flowing around the core
check.explain: In a high-bypass turbofan the big fan moves far more air around the core than through it, and that air makes most of the thrust.

reteach.label: Back to the very basics
reteach.intro: Let's slow right down and take the engine one step at a time.
steps: A piston moves up and down inside a cylinder.
Step 1, intake: the piston goes down and fuel and air rush in.
Step 2, compression: the piston goes up and squeezes them tight.
Step 3, power: a spark lights the mixture and the blast pushes the piston down hard.
Step 4, exhaust: the piston goes up and pushes the smoke out.
Then it starts again. A jet engine does the same four jobs, but all at once and continuously.
Intake: suck
Compression: squeeze
Power: bang
Exhaust: blow

visual.caption: The four strokes

example.stem: Which stroke actually pushes the airplane's propeller round?
steps: Only one stroke has burning fuel pushing the piston.
That is the power stroke.

reteach.hook: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow.

check.stem: In which stroke does fuel and air enter the cylinder?
check.explain: Intake: the piston moves down and draws in the fuel-air mixture.

check.stem: Which stroke comes right after compression?
check.explain: The order is intake, compression, power, exhaust.

check.stem: The altimeter shows the airplane's —
check.explain: The altimeter turns outside air pressure into height.

check.stem: What lights the fuel-air mixture in a piston engine?
check.explain: The spark plug, fed by an engine-driven magneto, fires near the end of the compression stroke.

units.title: Airspace, rules & airport operations
units.objective: Know airspace classes and VFR minimums, right-of-way, runway markings and lights, light-gun signals and transponder codes.

steps: Airspace: Class A, 18,000 ft MSL to FL600, IFR only. Class B, around the busiest airports: you need an ATC clearance. Class C: you need two-way radio contact. Class D, towered airports: two-way radio contact. Class E: other controlled airspace, including everything above FL600. Class G: uncontrolled.

VFR minimums: Class B is 3 SM and clear of clouds. C, D and E below 10,000 ft MSL: 3 SM, 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal. At or above 10,000 MSL: 5 SM, 1,000 below, 1,000 above, 1 SM horizontal. Class G by day at or below 1,200 AGL: 1 SM, clear of clouds.

Speed limits: 250 knots below 10,000 ft MSL; 200 knots under a Class B shelf, in a VFR corridor, or within 4 NM of a Class C/D primary airport at or below 2,500 AGL. VFR cruising above 3,000 AGL: magnetic course 0–179° flies odd thousands + 500, and 180–359° flies even thousands + 500.

Right-of-way: an aircraft in distress beats all. Then balloon > glider > airship > airplane or rotorcraft, with an aircraft towing or refueling ahead of other powered aircraft. Converging in the same category, the one on the right has the right-of-way. Head-on, both turn right. Overtaking, pass on the right. Landing, the lower aircraft has the right-of-way.

Airport: runway numbers are the magnetic heading to the nearest 10° with the last zero dropped (274° → 27). Runway markings are white, taxiway markings yellow. Hold short on the SOLID-line side. Lights: taxiway edge blue, taxiway centerline green, runway edge white. The beacon is white-green for a civil airport and two white flashes between greens for a military one. PAPI: two white and two red is on glide path.

Light gun, in flight: steady green = cleared to land, flashing green = return for landing, steady red = give way and keep circling, flashing red = airport unsafe. On the ground: steady green = cleared for takeoff, flashing green = cleared to taxi, steady red = stop, flashing red = taxi clear of the runway, flashing white = return to start. Squawk 7500 hijack, 7600 radio failure, 7700 emergency.
teach.formula: 75 taken alive · 76 radio fix · 77 going to heaven · Magnetic course 0–179° = odd + 500

worked.stem: A VFR pilot cruises at 6,500 ft MSL (4,000 ft AGL) on a magnetic course of 220° in Class E airspace. Is the altitude correct, and what are the cloud minimums?
steps: 220° falls in 180–359°, so the rule is EVEN thousands + 500: 4,500, 6,500, 8,500. 6,500 is correct.
6,500 MSL is below 10,000 MSL in Class E.
So the minimums are 3 SM visibility and 500 ft below, 1,000 ft above and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds.
worked.answer: Correct altitude; 3 SM, 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: Think of airspace as rooms in a building, each with its own door rule.
Class A is the top floor: instrument flying only.
Class B is the busiest room. You need permission (a clearance) to walk in.
Classes C and D just need you to talk first: two-way radio contact with the controller.
Class E is controlled but has no special door rule for VFR pilots. Class G is the uncontrolled room.
On the ground, white paint belongs to runways and yellow paint to taxiways. Blue lights line taxiways and white lights line runways.
Aircraft in distress
Balloon
Glider

units.title: Helicopters & naval aircraft
units.objective: Know the helicopter controls, torque, ETL and autorotation, and match the Navy and Marine Corps aircraft to their missions.

steps: Helicopter controls: the collective changes the pitch of all main-rotor blades together (climb and descend); the cyclic tilts the rotor disc (direction and airspeed); the pedals change tail-rotor pitch (heading); the throttle or governor holds rotor RPM.

Torque: with the main rotor turning counterclockwise from above (US designs), the fuselage tries to turn clockwise, nose right. More power needs more LEFT pedal. Translating tendency: tail-rotor thrust makes the helicopter drift in that direction in a hover.
Effective translational lift (ETL) comes in at about 16–24 knots, when the rotor flies into clean air. Ground effect works within about one rotor diameter. Retreating blade stall limits top speed.

Autorotation: after an engine failure the freewheeling unit disconnects the engine and air flowing UP through the rotor keeps it turning. First action: lower the collective to save rotor RPM. Then flare near the ground and cushion the landing with the collective.

Carrier aircraft: F/A-18E/F Super Hornet (strike fighter), F-35C (the carrier version of the F-35), EA-18G Growler (electronic attack), E-2D Hawkeye (airborne early warning), MH-60R (antisubmarine, HSM squadrons) and MH-60S (logistics and rescue, HSC squadrons), CMV-22B Osprey (carrier onboard delivery).

Shore-based and Marine aircraft: P-8A Poseidon (maritime patrol, a Boeing 737), E-6B Mercury (TACAMO, a 707). The Marines fly the F-35B (STOVL), MV-22B Osprey (tiltrotor), AH-1Z Viper and UH-1Y Venom. History: the F4U Corsair had gull wings, the F6F Hellcat scored the most WWII Navy kills, and the F-14 Tomcat had swing wings and the Phoenix missile.
teach.formula: Collective = up/down · Cyclic = direction · Pedals = heading · Engine out: collective DOWN

worked.stem: In a hover, a pilot of a US-design helicopter lowers the collective to descend without touching the pedals. Which way will the nose yaw, and why?
steps: Lowering the collective reduces blade pitch, so less power is needed.
Less power means less torque twisting the fuselage clockwise (nose right).
The tail rotor is still pushing as hard as before, so it now over-corrects.
The nose swings LEFT. The pilot needs right pedal to hold heading.
worked.answer: Left, because torque decreases while tail-rotor thrust stays the same

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: A helicopter pilot has a job for each hand and for the feet.
Left hand, the collective: pull up to go up, push down to go down.
Right hand, the cyclic: push it the way you want to move.
Feet, the pedals: they point the nose left or right using the little tail rotor.
The big rotor spinning one way makes the body want to spin the other way. The tail rotor stops that.
If the engine quits, the pilot lowers the collective at once, so the rotor keeps spinning like a maple seed falling.

reteach.intro: No problem. Let's link each helicopter idea to the part of the aircraft it comes from.
steps: Main rotor + collective: all blades change pitch together, which changes total lift.
Main rotor + cyclic: the disc tilts, which moves the helicopter in that direction.
Engine power → torque: the body twists opposite to the rotor. The tail rotor and pedals fight it, and the tail rotor's push causes translating tendency.
Airflow: in clean air above about 16–24 knots you get ETL, a lift boost. Too fast and the retreating blade stalls.
No engine: the freewheeling unit lets the rotor windmill. Collective down, flare, cushion.
Naval aircraft by mission: see far (E-2D), jam (EA-18G), hunt subs from the air base (P-8A), hunt subs from ships (MH-60R), fight and strike (F/A-18E/F, F-35C).

units.title: Ships, seamanship & rules of the road
units.objective: Use ship terms and compartment numbers, nautical units, buoys, navigation lights, sound signals and the COLREGs steering rules.

steps: Directions: bow (front), stern (back), port (left, red), starboard (right, green); forward, aft, amidships; athwartships = side to side. Inside the ship: deck = floor, bulkhead = wall, overhead = ceiling, ladder = stairs, hatch = an opening in a deck.

Hull measures: freeboard = waterline up to the main deck; draft = waterline down to the bottom of the keel; beam = greatest width; the keel is the backbone along the bottom. Units: knot = 1 nautical mile per hour; nautical mile ≈ 6,076 ft (1,852 m), one minute of latitude; fathom = 6 ft.

Compartment numbers (e.g. 2-75-3-L) read deck – frame – position – use. The main deck is 1, decks below are 2, 3…, and levels above are 01, 02…. The frame is the forward boundary. Position: 0 = centerline, odd = starboard, even = port. The letter is the use: L living, M ammunition, E engineering, A stores.

Steering rules (COLREGs): head-on, both alter to STARBOARD and pass port to port. Crossing, the vessel that has the other on its STARBOARD side gives way. Overtaking (from more than 22.5° abaft the beam), the overtaking vessel keeps clear. The give-way vessel acts early; the stand-on vessel holds course and speed.

Lights: masthead white over 225°, sidelights red (port) and green (starboard) over 112.5° each, sternlight white over 135°. If you see the other vessel's red light, it is on your starboard side and you give way. Sound: 1 short = turning to starboard, 2 = to port, 3 = astern propulsion, 5 or more = doubt or danger. In fog, power-driven making way = 1 prolonged blast at least every 2 minutes.

US buoys: 'red, right, returning' from sea. Red nuns carry even numbers and green cans odd numbers. Red-and-white vertical stripes = safe water. Day shapes: one ball = at anchor; two balls = not under command; three balls = aground; ball–diamond–ball = restricted in ability to maneuver.
teach.formula: Red, right, returning · Head-on: both to starboard · See red, give way · 1 short = starboard, 2 = port, 3 = astern

worked.stem: At night, steaming north, you see a white masthead light and a green sidelight on a power-driven vessel off your port bow. Who gives way?
steps: Seeing its GREEN (starboard) light means you are on its starboard side.
So it has you on ITS starboard side, which makes it the give-way vessel under Rule 15.
It is off your port bow: you have it on your port side, so you are the stand-on vessel.
You hold course and speed, ready to act if it doesn't give way.

The starboard light is green, like a traffic light that says go.
When two ships cross, the one that sees the other on its RIGHT (starboard) must give way, just like yielding at a crossroads.
If you see another ship's red light, that's a red stop light for you: you give way.
Coming home from sea, keep the red buoys on your right: 'red, right, returning'.

Crossing: other on your right?

units.title: Carrier ops, Navy organization & history
units.objective: Know flight-deck jerseys and launch and recovery gear, the squadron–air wing–strike group chain, aviation ratings, and the milestones of naval aviation.

steps: Flight-deck jerseys: YELLOW = handling, catapult and arresting gear officers and plane directors ('shooter' included). GREEN = catapult and arresting gear crews and maintainers. RED = ordnance and crash and salvage. PURPLE = fuel ('grapes'). BLUE = plane handlers, chocks and chains, tractors and elevators. BROWN = plane captains. WHITE = safety, medical, LSOs and squadron inspectors.

Launch: the aircraft is hooked to a catapult (steam on Nimitz-class carriers, electromagnetic EMALS on Ford-class) while a jet blast deflector (JBD) rises behind it. Recovery: the tailhook catches an arresting wire (a 'trap'). The pilot goes to FULL power at touchdown in case of a bolter, a miss of every wire.

On approach the pilot flies the 'meatball' of the Fresnel lens optical landing system: ball above the green datum lights = high, below = low. The landing signal officer (LSO, 'Paddles') can order a wave-off. The angled deck lets a bolter fly off clear of parked aircraft. The air boss runs the deck and nearby airspace from Pri-Fly; the handler plots aircraft on the 'Ouija board'.

Organization: squadrons (each led by a commander, O-5) form a carrier air wing (CVW) led by the CAG, a captain (O-6). The air wing embarks on the carrier, which sails with escorts as a carrier strike group led by a rear admiral. Squadron letters: VFA strike fighter, VAQ electronic attack, VAW early warning, HSC/HSM helicopters, VP patrol.

Enlisted aviation ratings start with A: AD engines, AM airframes and hydraulics, AE electrical, AT avionics, AO ordnance, AG weather (aerographer's mate), AC air traffic control. Aviation boatswain's mates: ABE launch and recovery gear, ABF fuel, ABH aircraft handling. Exception: PR, aircrew survival equipment (parachutes).

History: Eugene Ely took off from USS Birmingham (Nov 1910) and landed on USS Pennsylvania (Jan 1911). Naval aviation's birthday is May 8, 1911 (the Curtiss A-1 Triad). USS Langley (CV-1, 1922) was a converted collier. 1942: Doolittle's B-25s flew from Hornet (April), Coral Sea was the first battle with no ship sighting the enemy (May), and at Midway SBDs sank four Japanese carriers (June). The Blue Angels began in 1946, the first US jet carrier landing was the XFD-1 Phantom (1946), and USS Enterprise (CVN-65, 1961) was the first nuclear carrier.

units.title: Airspeeds, weights & aircraft lighting
units.objective: Step from indicated to true airspeed, ground speed and Mach, read the airspeed-indicator markings and V-speeds, turn fluid volumes into pounds, and read another aircraft's lights at night.

steps: Airspeed in order, 'ICE-T': INDICATED (straight off the dial) → CALIBRATED (corrected for instrument and position error, largest when slow with flaps down) → EQUIVALENT (corrected for compressibility, which matters only at high speed and altitude) → TRUE (corrected for altitude and nonstandard temperature: your real speed through the air).

Thin air presses less on the pitot tube, so at altitude TAS is higher than IAS, roughly 2% per 1,000 feet. Ground speed is TAS corrected for wind: a headwind subtracts, a tailwind adds. Mach = TAS ÷ the local speed of sound, which depends only on temperature (about 661 knots at standard sea level), so colder air gives a higher Mach at the same TAS.

Airspeed indicator: white arc from VSO (stall, landing configuration) to VFE (max flaps extended). Green arc from VS1 (stall, clean) to VNO (max structural cruising). Yellow arc from VNO to VNE: smooth air only, with caution. Red line at VNE: never exceed. Light twins add a red radial line (VMC) and a blue radial line (VYSE).

Unmarked V-speeds: VA, design maneuvering speed, which goes DOWN as weight goes down; VX, best angle of climb (most height per distance, to clear obstacles); VY, best rate of climb (most height per minute); VLE and VLO, landing gear extended and operating.

Planning weights (FAA Weight & Balance Handbook): avgas 6 lb/gal, jet fuel about 6.7 lb/gal (JP-5 about 6.8), oil 7.5 lb/gal (4 quarts to the gallon), water about 8.35 lb/gal. Useful load = maximum weight − basic empty weight. Moment = weight × arm, and CG = total moment ÷ total weight.

Aircraft lights: red position light on the LEFT wingtip, green on the RIGHT, white on the tail. Each wingtip light covers 110° forward and the tail light 140° aft. Position lights are required from sunset to sunrise; anti-collision lights (red beacon or white strobes) whenever installed, but the pilot may turn them off when that is safer, such as in cloud (14 CFR 91.209).
teach.formula: ICE-T: Indicated → Calibrated → Equivalent → True → (wind) → Ground · Avgas 6 · Jet 6.7 · Oil 7.5 · Water 8.35 lb/gal

worked.stem: An airplane cruises at 160 knots indicated at 6,000 feet into a 20-knot headwind. Using the 2%-per-1,000-feet rule, estimate its true airspeed and ground speed.
steps: 160 × 1.12 ≈ 179 knots true airspeed.
A headwind subtracts from ground speed: 179 − 20 = 159 knots.
The trap is changing the TAS for wind. Indicated and true airspeed are measured relative to the air; only ground speed feels the wind.
worked.answer: About 179 knots TAS and 159 knots ground speed

alt.label: Let's go really slowly
steps: The airspeed needle measures how hard the air pushes into a small tube on the wing, the pitot tube. That reading is indicated airspeed.
Higher up the air is thinner, so it pushes less hard and the needle reads LESS than the speed you are really moving through the air.
Your real speed through the air is true airspeed. Add or subtract the wind and you get ground speed, your speed over the map.
Fuel is measured in gallons, but an airplane cares about pounds. Avgas weighs 6 pounds a gallon; jet fuel a little more.
At night another airplane's lights show which way it points: red on its left wing, green on its right wing, white on its tail.
See red on your right and green on your left? It is coming straight at you.

Calibrated: errors fixed
Equivalent: compressibility
True: altitude, temp
Ground: wind

options: indicated airspeed ÷ the speed of sound at sea level
ground speed ÷ the local speed of sound

reteach.label: Let's try it another way
reteach.intro: No problem. Let's tie every speed, weight and light to the question it answers.
steps: 'What does the needle say?' Indicated airspeed. 'What would a perfect instrument say?' Calibrated. 'What is my real speed through the air?' True. 'How fast am I crossing the map?' Ground speed.
'Why is true faster than indicated up high?' Thinner air presses less on the pitot tube. Rule of thumb: add about 2% per 1,000 feet.
'How close am I to the speed of sound?' Mach = TAS ÷ the local speed of sound. Sound travels slower in cold air, so the same TAS is a higher Mach up high.
'Where can I fly?' The colors: white = flaps allowed, green = normal, yellow = smooth air only, red line = never.
'How heavy is it?' Multiply gallons by the fluid's weight: avgas 6, jet fuel 6.7, oil 7.5, water 8.35. Turn quarts into gallons first (÷ 4).
'Which way is it pointing?' Red is its left wingtip, green its right, white its tail. Only white means you are behind it.
Needle: indicated
Perfect needle: calibrated
Through the air: true
Over the map: ground

units.title: Naval vessels, hull codes & Navy history
units.objective: Decode hull classification symbols, match each ship type to its job, and put the key dates, battles and figures of US Navy history in order.

steps: Hull symbols are built from letters: CV = aircraft carrier, CG = cruiser, DD = destroyer, FF = frigate, SS = submarine, L = amphibious. Add N for nuclear power (CVN, SSN), G for guided missiles (CG, DDG, FFG, SSGN) and B for ballistic missiles (SSBN). A 'T-' prefix (T-AO, T-AKE) marks a Military Sealift Command ship with a mostly civilian crew.

Surface combatants, traditionally largest to smallest: carrier (Nimitz and Ford classes, about 100,000 tons), cruiser (CG, Ticonderoga class), destroyer (DDG, Arleigh Burke class, the backbone of the surface fleet), frigate (FFG). The Ticonderoga cruisers and Burke destroyers are built around the Aegis combat system. LCS = littoral combat ship, for shallow coastal waters.

Submarines: SSN = nuclear attack submarine (Virginia, Los Angeles and Seawolf classes) that hunts ships and other subs; SSBN = ballistic-missile submarine (Ohio class) for nuclear deterrence; SSGN = guided-missile submarine, four Ohios converted to carry Tomahawks. Amphibious: LHA and LHD assault ships look like small carriers and fly F-35Bs, MV-22s and helicopters; LPD = amphibious transport dock; LSD = dock landing ship. LHDs, LPDs and LSDs have well decks that launch LCAC hovercraft.

Founding: Continental Navy, October 13, 1775 (the Navy's birthday; the Marines' is November 10, 1775). John Paul Jones, 'I have not yet begun to fight' (Bonhomme Richard vs. HMS Serapis, 1779). The Naval Act of 1794 ordered six frigates, including USS Constitution, launched 1797 and still the world's oldest commissioned warship afloat. Department of the Navy, 1798. Naval Academy at Annapolis, 1845.

1800s: James Lawrence, 'Don't give up the ship' (USS Chesapeake, 1813), the words Oliver Hazard Perry flew at Lake Erie before reporting 'We have met the enemy and they are ours.' USS Monitor vs. CSS Virginia, the first ironclad battle (Hampton Roads, 1862). David Farragut, 'Damn the torpedoes!' (Mobile Bay, 1864), later the first full admiral. The Great White Fleet sailed around the world in 1907–1909.

1900s: Lt. Theodore Ellyson became Naval Aviator No. 1 (1911). Pearl Harbor, December 7, 1941. Midway, June 1942: Japan lost Akagi, Kaga, Soryu and Hiryu. Leyte Gulf, October 1944, often called the largest naval battle in history. Japan surrendered aboard USS Missouri on September 2, 1945. USS Nautilus signaled 'Underway on nuclear power' in 1955 and passed under the North Pole in 1958; Adm. Hyman Rickover led the nuclear Navy. Naval aviator Alan Shepard became the first American in space in 1961.

worked.stem: Decode SSGN and LHD, and say which one could launch a hovercraft full of Marines.
steps: SSGN: SS = submarine, G = guided missile, N = nuclear. A nuclear-powered guided-missile submarine, a converted Ohio carrying Tomahawks.
LHD: L = amphibious, H = helicopter, D = dock (a well deck). An amphibious assault ship.
Flooding the LHD's well deck lets LCAC hovercraft and landing craft drive out loaded with Marines.
So the LHD is the one. The trap is reading N or G as size or role: they only describe power and weapons.
worked.answer: SSGN: nuclear guided-missile submarine; LHD: amphibious assault ship, the one with the well deck
